paper_metadata.title: Encoding of Probability Distributions for Quantum Monte Carlo Using Tensor Networks

summary: The paper studies tensor-network-based probability loading for quantum Monte Carlo, using TT-cross to encode log-normal distributions into quantum circuits. It reports a 5-qubit IBM Eagle R3 hardware demonstration for the univariate case, with KS distance reaching 7.2×10^-5 at 16 qubits in simulation, and multivariate benchmarks up to 5 dimensions with KL divergence around 10^-2 in the worst case. The main quantitative claim is improved circuit-depth scalability versus Grover-Rudolph state preparation, but no practical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Univariate log-normal probability distribution encoding with TT-cross, evaluated by KS distance and training time across qubit counts and bond dimensions; includes simulator-based circuit generation and a 5-qubit IBM Eagle R3 hardware run.

algorithm.variant: TT-cross tensor-network state preparation mapped to quantum circuits; Grover-Rudolph baseline comparison

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Probability distribution discretized into 2^d points and encoded on d qubits; TT-cross used to approximate the distribution and then mapped to a quantum circuit. For the univariate case, the paper uses binary discretization of the log-normal distribution over increasing qubit counts.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Approximate a target univariate log-normal probability distribution with minimal KS distance between target and encoded distribution.

problem_instance.description: Univariate log-normal distribution calibrated from real market data for financial instrument pricing.

dataset_specification.description: Log-normal distribution parameters calibrated using real market data; exact ticker/date range not reported.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Distribution discretized to 2^d points; TT-cross approximation used to build tensor-train representation; no further preprocessing details reported.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: KS distance and average training time reported as functions of number of qubits; hardware run executed 10,000 shots; comparison against Qiskit built-in Grover-Rudolph state preparation.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: TT-cross approximation used to construct tensor-train representation of the target distribution; then Algorithm 1 maps TT cores to unitary gates.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement outcomes compared to target empirical distribution; KS distance computed.

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic scaling in training complexity; linear scaling in circuit depth
speedup_claims.conditions: for probability distribution loading via TT-cross mapped to quantum circuits
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports qualitative scaling and plots, but no exact crossover point or constant factors.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Circuit depth scales linearly with number of qubits; training complexity scales logarithmically with number of discretization points.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Qiskit built-in Grover-Rudolph state preparation scales linearly with number of discretization points, implying exponential scaling with qubits.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: At least a fault-tolerant or substantially lower-noise implementation would be needed; the paper only reports a 5-qubit IBM Eagle R3 run and does not demonstrate end-to-end advantage over classical methods.
limiting_factors: Noise degrades results at higher optimization level
No end-to-end runtime advantage over classical loading is shown
The main bottleneck is state preparation / probability loading

notes: The paper explicitly reports a 5-qubit IBM Eagle R3 hardware experiment, but does not state the total qubit register size for the hardware device beyond that experiment; num_qubits is therefore inferred as 5 for the hardware run. Circuit depth is discussed qualitatively and via plots, but no exact numeric depth is given in text.

The paper reports a small hardware demonstration on IBM Eagle R3 but does not claim practical quantum advantage; it emphasizes improved circuit scalability of the TT method over Grover-Rudolph state preparation.

experiments.description: Qiskit built-in Grover-Rudolph state preparation baseline for univariate log-normal distribution, compared against the TT-cross method in circuit depth and training complexity.
key_results: Circuit depth scales exponentially with qubit count for the Qiskit/Grover-Rudolph method, while the TT approach scales linearly.
Training complexity scales linearly with the number of discretization points for the Qiskit method, versus logarithmically for the TT approach.
